A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same NAG research. Their complete main texts and appendices are available, and visual inspection resolves equation-extraction artifacts. Figures, tables, and relocated material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v3 reports original benchmark evaluations, a human preference and rating study, guidance-coefficient sensitivity experiments, and generation-order comparisons.

after.justification: v4 retains those original results and adds caption-count, event-category, cross-dataset, alternative-baseline, and ControlFoley evaluations.

M1.justification: The NAG equation, MMAudio/ControlNet architecture, flow-matching objective, non-overlapping training pairs, and sequential generation procedure remain unchanged. The ControlFoley experiment applies NAG to another backbone without documenting a new algorithmic component.

E1.justification: v4 expands evaluation beyond Multi-Caps VGGSound to human, audio-aware captions in VGGSounder, the AudioCaps test set, and Movie Gen Audio Bench (Section 5.3; Appendix J). AudioCaps was already a training source in v3, but its evaluation use is new. Training dataset coverage is retained.

E2.justification: The original comparator sets remain in Tables 1-2. v4 adds fused-caption MMAudio followed by AudioSep, independent AudioX text-to-audio generation, and ControlFoley evaluated with and without NAG (Tables A2, A3, A7). These introduce substantially different comparison approaches.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs separate VGGSounder videos into subsets with 2-5 captions and aggregate separability by 309 event labels. The original eight-second, five-track evaluation, metrics, training settings, and human-study sample sizes remain unchanged. These are additional protocols, rather than revisions demonstrating reruns of existing experiments.

E4.justification: Section 5.3 newly examines effectiveness across caption-count subsets. Appendix E tests whether separability gains extend across event categories, and Appendix K examines dependence on the MMAudio backbone. These substantially extend the retained guidance-strength and generation-order analyses.

E5.justification: v4 replaces rating standard deviations with 95% confidence intervals and adds Wilson preference intervals with evenly split ties (Appendix A; Tables 3-4), without increasing the reported responses. However, the preference widths are inconsistent with the stated calculation: 50 responses imply approximately ±11.97 percentage points for audio quality, versus the reported ±7.71.

E6.justification: Main Tables 1-2 and sensitivity scores are retained. v4 adds caption-count and category findings, derived preference summaries, and results for new datasets, comparators, and ControlFoley. For example, Table A7 reports ControlFoley CLAP A-A of 60.67 without NAG and 53.81 with it. The existing random-order DeSync entry changes from 0.42 to 0.43 (v3 Table A3; v4 Table A4).

T1.justification: The concept-negation assumption, probability factorization, guidance equations, and Appendix B derivation retain the same mathematics. Added training explanations are conceptual. Incorrect equation cross-references introduced in v4 do not constitute a substantive change to the derivation.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction narrow the framing from comprehensively covering all relevant sound events to authoring multiple complementary tracks. The central claims about NAG, training with single-reference datasets, separability, and composite quality remain; the new contribution list largely consolidates them.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive explanations of shared acoustic context and avoidance of waveform copying, and clarifies why visually plausible captions need not reproduce recorded audio. New discussions interpret event-dependent gains, source-separation failures, and the text-alignment versus audiovisual-alignment tradeoff. The original base-model and mixing limitations are retained in Appendix M.

D1.justification: v4 adds a project-page URL, replacing the local supplementary demo instruction, and discloses AudioSep's default configuration, caption reuse, and GPT-5 label assignment. It also clarifies that the sensitivity sweep shares a random generation order. Existing architecture, optimizer, training-budget, hardware, and timing details are retained.

R1.justification: Related work adds focused comparisons with ReWaS, SelVA, and SonicVisionLM, alongside references supporting new benchmarks and comparison methods. These extend the existing positioning around negative audio conditioning and generative addition without fundamentally redefining the claimed novelty. Publication variants of existing references are not distinct new works.

P1.justification: v4 edits the abstract and introduction, adds contribution bullets and explanatory paragraphs, swaps the model and dataset appendices, and moves limitations to the end. Much existing prose and the main narrative order remain recognizable. Appendix B also introduces incorrect main-equation references.

P2.justification: v4 changes document-wide typography, margins, headers, table formatting, and caption placement, while adding several result tables and the caption-count plot. v3 Figure 5 moves to v4 Figure A1, and rating Table A1 becomes main Table 4. Existing method diagrams and spectrogram examples retain their substantive content.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially addresses v3's narrow validation on one automatically captioned benchmark and one proposed-method backbone. Human-captioned evaluation, additional datasets, alternative generation comparisons, and ControlFoley tests strengthen evidence for generality and the practical value of sequential generation. Clearer task framing also helps interpretation. Sparse details for some new experiments, incorrect cross-references, and inconsistent preference confidence intervals limit the gains, but do not outweigh the substantially broader empirical support.
